After developing with 9...Bg4 and 10...O-O, White asked a question with 11.h3. Instead of retreating or playing 11...Bf6, you played 11...Kh8, allowing 12.hxg4 where White simply won a piece.

review.focus: Always respond to direct threats against your pieces; on 11.h3, moving the bishop with 11...Bf6 keeps the position fully balanced.

sections.text: You opened with the Italian and 3.Bc4 3...Nf6, then played 4.Nxe5, a blunder that left a piece to be won (4.Ng5 was the safer try). After 4...Nxe5 5.Bb3 Black missed the best reply, and 5...Bc5 allowed 6.d4!, which forked the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5.

6...Nf3+ was another error, and 7.Qxf3 7...Bxd4 8.Bg5 left you under pressure; 8.Qd1 was better. Black returned the favour with 8...O-O, missing 8...Bxb2. You castled long with 10.O-O-O and brought a knight to 11.Nd5.

11...Bg4 was a mistake that let you win the queen with 12.Qxg4 12...Nxg4 13.Bxd8, but 13...Nxf2 forked your two rooks on d1 and h1. 14.Nxc7 was a blunder (14.Bxc7 was better), and 16.Ne6 missed 16.Rxh1. Still, 17.Nxf8 was the best reply, and 18.Rxh1 restored the balance.

The endgame was where you won it. 28...a5 gave you chances, 29.cxb5! and 32.b6! created a dangerous passed pawn, and 40.b8=Q ended the fight. 31.Kf3 was a slip but did not matter; 47.Qf7# finished the game with mate.

review.turning_point: 28...a5 allowed 29.cxb5!, and 32.b6! then created a passed pawn that decided the game.
review.focus: 4.Nxe5 grabbed a pawn and left a piece to be won. In the Italian, remember the knight on e5 can be recaptured by 4...Nxe5, so 4.Ng5 or a quiet developing move kept the position safe.

sections.text: When your opponent went for the risky 5...Nxd5, you didn't hesitate. You punished the move immediately with 6.Nxf7, setting up a brutal fork on d8 and h8 that dragged the enemy king into the open.

Black cracked under the pressure on d5 with 8...Nd4, and your 9.Bxd5+ took full advantage of the pin on d5. After Black blundered with 9...Qxd5, 10.Qxd5+ snapped up the queen, leaving Black completely lost.
You wrapped things up flawlessly. Rather than worrying about your rook on a1, you mobilized every piece with 14.O-O, 17.d4, and 18.Bg5+, forcing resignation.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange where you punished 7...h6 and converted a huge edge

sections.text: You played the Exchange Variation, taking with 3.exd5 and developing 4.Nc3 and 5.Bg5. Black's 5...Bg4 6.Nf3 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 left you with an active queen on f3 eyeing the d5 pawn.

Black's 7...h6 was the big mistake (+0.2 to +3.0), and you found the best reply with 8.Bxf6. After 8...exf6 you played 9.Qxd5 and Black's queen trade 9...Qxd5 10.Nxd5 left a huge position for you. 10...Nc6 was another error.
11.Nc7+ was the tactic that decided the game: it forked the king on e8 and the rook on a8. After 11...Kd7 12.Nxa8 you were far ahead in material. You then took some care with 13.Nb6+ and 14.O-O-O.

When Black grabbed with 19...Bxh2, you trapped it with 20.g3, 21.Rh1 and 22.Rxh2, which restored your lead. The rest was technique: 26.Rxd8, 31.Bxe4+ and 35.R8xe4+ kept simplifying, and the win came after 47 moves. A 97 percent accuracy says it all.

review.turning_point: 7...h6 gave you 8.Bxf6, and 11.Nc7+ then forked the king and the rook on a8.
review.focus: You played almost flawlessly. Keep the habit of looking for the forcing capture first, as with 8.Bxf6 and 11.Nc7+, in every position where the opponent has just weakened something.

review.headline: A clean queenless Petrov where the engine liked your side the whole way

sections.text: You played the Petrov and met 3.d3 with 3...d5 and 4.Bg5 with 4...dxe4. After 5.Bxf6 5...gxf6 6.dxe4 you traded queens with 6...Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1, which cost White the right to castle. That is a good practical decision: White's king ends up stuck in the centre.

You developed with 7...Bg4, 8...Bh6 and 9...Bd7, then castled long with 11...O-O-O. White's 12.Ke1 tidied the king, and you used the f-pawn with 12...f5 to challenge the centre. Accuracy 95 percent shows how few real mistakes there were.

White went wrong with 13.exf5, which let you recapture with 13...Bxf5 and put an active bishop on the c2 pawn. 14.Rd1 was another inaccuracy, since 14.Bd3 was the engine's line, and you found 14...Bxc2, grabbing a pawn.

After 15.Rxd8+ 15...Rxd8 you were a clean pawn up and the engine rated you at +3.5. The record shows the game ended as a loss by resignation, so check carefully that you were not too hasty at the end.

review.turning_point: 13.exf5 and 14.Rd1 were White's errors, and you punished the second with 14...Bxc2.
review.focus: There was little to fix in your play. After 15...Rxd8 you were better, so make a habit of checking the evaluation and the material count before ever resigning.

review.headline: A Petrov where a queenside pawn move and the clock cost you a good position

sections.text: You played the main Petrov line with 3.Nxe5, 4.Nf3 and 6.c4, building a small space edge with 7.d5 before Black castled with 7...O-O. The opening was fine at about +0.4.

8.Bg5 was a little loose, and 9.Be3 was the real mistake (-2.0); 9.Be2 was cleaner. Your opponent's 9...Bg4 pinned your knight on f3 to the queen, and it was an error as well: 9...Ng4 was the strong move. After 10.Be2 and 11.O-O you were back to normal.

From there you played well. 13.h3 13...Bh5 14.Nc3 and 15.Qb3 built up your queenside play, and 17.Rfe1 put a rook on the e-file. 18.Bb5 pinned the d7 knight against the rook on e8, though the engine felt it was a touch loose. 18...Bxf3 19.gxf3 damaged your structure, and 20.Rad1 was a touch passive.
21.f4 was the final slip (+0.4 to -0.9). 21.Be2 kept things safe, whereas 21.f4 opened the position for 21...Nf3+. You then lost on time, so a roughly equal middlegame went unplayed.

review.turning_point: 9.Be3 cost you nearly two pawns of evaluation before the opponent returned it with 9...Bg4, and the later 21.f4 loosened your king.
review.focus: 21.f4 pushed a pawn in front of your king when 21.Be2 was calm. Keep pawn moves near your own king to a minimum, and play faster in quiet positions so you have time later.

review.headline: A Petrov where the opponent drifted and you collected material with your queen

sections.text: This was a quiet Petrov with a kingside fianchetto for White. Both sides developed naturally with 4.g3 4...Bg4 5.Bg2 5...Be7 and castled, and the evaluation hovered around zero until 9...Qc7 gave you a small edge. White's 10.Nb3 was careful and the position stayed balanced.

10...d5 was the one inaccurate move of the opening, dropping you to -1.4. The engine liked 10...a5 first. White did not punish it: 11.Bd2 threw away the advantage and 11.cxd5 was the move. After 12.cxd5 12...cxd5 you were back to equality.

Then White went wrong in a big way. 13.Qd1 was a blunder, and your 13...Qc2 gave some of it back; the engine wanted 13...dxe4 first. But 14.Qe1 was worse still, missing 14.Qxc2, and from here you were up in material and in control.

You took it from there confidently. 14...dxe4 and 15...Qxb2 opened the queenside, 17...Qxa2 grabbed more, and 18...Bxf3 followed by 19...Rxd2 kept the pressure on. By 25...Qxb1+ and 26...Rxf2+ White's position was collapsing, and 31...Qxe4 ended it.

review.turning_point: 14.Qe1 missed the simple 14.Qxc2, and from then on you were winning material with every move.
review.focus: 13...Qc2 jumped into the opponent's camp when 13...dxe4 first kept everything safe. Before sending the queen deep, check whether you can win the same thing with a simple pawn capture.

review.headline: A London System where you were better in the middle, then let a mate slip away

sections.text: You met the London with 1...d5 and 2...e6 and had no trouble. You traded bishops with 3...Bd6 4.Bxd6 4...cxd6, answered 6.Nc3 with 6...Ne4, and after 7.Nxe4 7...dxe4 8.Nd2 8...d5 the position was level. White's queen sortie with 9.Qg4 and 11.Qh5 plus 10.O-O-O looked threatening but was slow, and after 12.exd4 you stood clearly better (+1.4).

The first slip was 13...Qc7, which dropped you to -1.2. The engine preferred 13...f5, keeping e4 solid. White immediately gave it back with 14.f3, missing the strong 14.Qxd5. After 14...Nxd4 you were fine again, but 16...g6 was the real damage (+0.9 to -4.1). 16...Qf4+ would have forked the king on c1 and the knight on e4.
You deserve credit for 17...Kg7, the only good answer to 17.Nf6+. Even so, 18.Qxh7+ and 20.Qxd4+ left White with the initiative, and you were worse for the rest of the game.

The saddest moment came at 23.Qf6, when White overreached. 23...Qf4+ 24.Rd2 would have led to a forced mate, but 23...Bxg4 let the chance go. 24.Rxd8 was a mistake and you found 24...Rxd8, yet 25.Rf1 was met by 25...Qe7, which walked into a skewer on the e7 queen and d8 rook. 25...Bh5 was the way out.

review.turning_point: 23.Qf6 gave you a forced mate with 23...Qf4+ 24.Rd2, but 23...Bxg4 grabbed a pawn instead and swung the game from winning to losing.
review.focus: At 23...Bxg4 you reached for a capture when a check was available. Before every move in a sharp position, list all your checks first; 23...Qf4+ was one of them.

review.headline: A textbook Fried Liver attack cut short by the clock

sections.text: In the Italian Game, your opponent walked right into trouble with 5...Nxd5?. You pounced with the classic 6.Nxf7!, executing a clean fork on the black queen and rook that dragged their king out into the open.

After Black retreated with 7...Ke8?, you kept maximum pressure with 8.Bxd5!. Following 8...Qe7?, you played 9.Bxc6+!, exploiting the pin on the b7-pawn, which allowed you to pick up the loose rook with 11.Qxa8 and reach a crushing +5.2 evaluation.

review.turning_point: Black's 5...Nxd5? allowed your devastating sacrifice 6.Nxf7!, completely tearing open the enemy king and winning decisive material.
review.focus: Your tactical execution was flawless, but in bullet you need to convert winning positions rapidly before flagging; practice blitzing out safe development once you are a full rook ahead as after 11.Qxa8.

review.headline: A sharp queenside push undone by a costly oversight

sections.text: You stepped into a Classical Pirc and pushed 5.e5?! early, which triggered queens coming off with 6...Qxd1+ and left your e5-pawn vulnerable. After losing the pawn to 8...Nxe5, you looked for queenside counterplay. When Black slipped with 13...Bh3?, you punished it immediately with 14.a5!, driving their knight back to c8 and regaining control.

Right after creating momentum, disaster struck with 15.b3??, which left the a1-rook undefended. Black snapped it up with 15...Bxa1, costing you an entire rook. You tried to complicate matters with 17.Nd5 and 18.Nc7, but you ultimately ran out of time in a tough position.

review.turning_point: 15.b3?? dropped the rook on a1 to 15...Bxa1, throwing away the pressure you built with 14.a5! and handing Black a decisive material lead.
review.focus: Always check your long diagonals for loose pieces before moving flank pawns, as 15.b3 left your rook hanging on a1.

review.headline: A King's Gambit win that you took over with 12...Bxd4 and 15...Ne3+ and finished with 40...Qe1#

sections.text: This was a King's Gambit Accepted and you took the pawn with 2...exf4. After 3.Nf3 d5 4.e5 you had a good position (+1.9 for you). 4...f6 was the weaker answer, since 4...g5 was best, and 5...c5?? was a blunder when 5...fxe5 was available.
You recovered well with 6...Bg4, 7...Qb6 and 8...Bxc5, and after 9.Be2 Bf2+ 10.Kf1 you had your pieces working. 10...fxe5? gave a little back, since 10...Nc6 was best.

12.Bd4?? looked like a fork of your queen and bishop, but 12...Bxd4! simply took it, and 13.cxd4 Qxb2 left you a pawn up with White's king stuck in the middle. Then 15.Ne5?? gave you 15...Ne3+!, forking the king and queen. After 16.Kf2 Nxd1+ you were up about ten.
From there you converted cleanly: 17...Qxd4+, 18...Bxe2, 22.Rxd5 and a long chase of the king ended with 40...Qe1#.

review.turning_point: 15...Ne3+ forked the king and queen and won the white queen.
review.focus: 5...c5 gave up your advantage in the opening. Before a pawn push, check the pawn you can take: 5...fxe5 6.dxe5 kept control.

review.headline: A sharp Colle System derailed by tactical oversights

sections.text: You developed smoothly against the Colle System, but your pawn break with 11...f6 allowed White to hop in with 12.Nd4. After 12...fxe5 13.Nxe6 Qe8 14.Nxf8 Qxf8, you lost an exchange and were forced onto the defensive.

The position exploded into mutual tactics on move 18. White played 18.Qd4, which set up a pin on your d7-knight. You responded with 18...b5, trapping the light-squared bishop, but White counterpunched with 20.Bxd5+, pinning your c6-pawn to the rook on a8.

The decisive error came when you recaptured with 22...Qxf6 instead of 22...Nxf6. This left your d7-knight completely undefended, allowing 23.Qxd7. After 25.Qd5, White targeted both your bishop and the loose rook on a8, wrapping up the game with 26.Qxa8+.

review.turning_point: Playing 22...Qxf6 left your d7-knight hanging, allowing White to take it on move 23 and control the entire board.
review.focus: Always check which pieces are left undefended before recapturing, as missing the defense of your knight on 22...Qxf6 cost you the game.

review.headline: A sharp knight hop punishes White's reckless flank attack

sections.text: You handled the Queen's Gambit Declined well, though 4...cxd6? compromised your pawn structure when 4...Qxd6 was cleaner. You mobilized smoothly afterwards, anchoring central control while White tried to push aggressively on the kingside.
White got careless with 15.h6??, neglecting their queen entirely. You pounced immediately with 15...Nxd3+!, winning the queen and dismantling White's position.
From there, you converted ruthlessly. You invaded the queenside, captured the rook with 23...Bxa2, took complete control of the c-file with 30...Rc2, and wrapped up a clean checkmate.

review.turning_point: The game flipped decisively on 15.h6??, which allowed 15...Nxd3+!, removing White's queen and giving you total control.
review.focus: Watch your pawn structure when recapturing on d6; 4...cxd6? doubled your pawns unnecessarily when 4...Qxd6 developed naturally.

review.headline: A sharp kingside breakthrough leads to a queen win

sections.text: Black immediately compromised their kingside with 1...f6, giving you the center with 2.d4. After an early skirmish on e5, 5.Nxe5 handed Black an opportunity, but Black missed it with 5...d6, and you retreated with 6.Nf3 to stay ahead.

Black's position crumbled after 9...Nf6, which you punished immediately with 10.exf6 to win material. Following 12.Ne5+, Black played 12...fxe5, which ran directly into a discovered attack on the queen with 13.Bxd8.
With the queen secured, you simplified the position cleanly. You exchanged rooks, pushed your passed h-pawn to promote with 36.h8=Q, and cleanly wrapped up the game with 69.Qh1#.

review.turning_point: Black's 9...Nf6 gave away the game, allowing 10.exf6 to shatter Black's kingside and win material.
review.focus: Calculate tactical consequences before capturing central pawns, as 5.Nxe5 gave Black an immediate chance to equalize.
